Steal
steel
v.t. (to take another's property without right; rendering Hebrew ganab, Greek klepto)
Old English stelan. The eighth commandment's Hebrew ganab covers taking by stealth as distinct from robbery by force, and it is the root of the New Testament kleptes — a thief who comes unseen rather than a robber who comes armed.

Biblical Definition

The eighth commandment is two words in Hebrew and three in English: “Thou shalt not steal” (Exodus 20:15). Its brevity conceals how much it establishes. A commandment against theft presupposes property that can be stolen, and so Scripture's law code assumes and protects private ownership — a man's field, house, ox, and cloak are genuinely his, and the same law obliges him to leave gleanings, lend without usury to a poor brother, and release debts in the seventh year. Paul gives the commandment its full New Testament shape, which is not merely a prohibition but a reversal: “Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth” (Ephesians 4:28). The thief's repentance is a three-stage movement — stop taking, start working, and work in order to give — so that the man ends as a source where he began as a drain. Agur's prayer supplies the pastoral realism, asking for neither poverty nor riches because each has its own temptation: “Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain” (Proverbs 30:9). And the Lord Jesus identifies theft as the mark of the false shepherd: the thief cometh not but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy (John 10:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

To take what is another's. The eighth commandment presupposes and protects real property; Paul turns the thief into a giver by way of work; Agur prays against both riches and poverty because each has its own temptation to theft.

expand to see more

STEAL, v.t. [Sax. stelan.] To take and carry away feloniously, as the personal goods of another. To constitute stealing, the taking must be felonious, that is, with an intent to take what belongs to another, and without his consent.

2. To withdraw or convey without notice or clandestinely.

3. To gain or win by address or gradual and imperceptible means; as, to steal the affections.

STEAL, v.i. To withdraw or pass privily; to slip along or away unperceived.

5. To practice theft; to take feloniously. Thou shalt not steal. Ex. 20.

Key Scripture

Exodus 20:15 — "Thou shalt not steal."

Ephesians 4:28 — "Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth."

Proverbs 30:9 — "Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain."

John 10:10 — "The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly."

Modern Corruption

Theft is redefined by category — taking from the wealthy, from a corporation, or from the state is reclassified as recovery or protest — and in the opposite direction, the commandment is treated as though it protected property absolutely, with no obligation attached to its use.

expand to see more

The most common modern erosion of the eighth commandment is jurisdictional: the thing taken is said not to be really owned, or the owner said not to deserve it, and the taking becomes redistribution, shrinkage, or a blow struck against a system. Scripture recognises no such exemption. It does insist, relentlessly, that the wealthy owe the poor — gleanings, interest-free loans, the seventh-year release, prompt wages, open-handedness — but it establishes those as duties on the owner, not as licences for the taker. The distinction matters practically: a duty enforced by conscience and community produces generosity, and a licence to take produces a society in which nothing is secure and the poor suffer first, since they have the least margin and the least protection. Zacchaeus is Scripture's model of a rich man converted, and his restitution is fourfold and voluntary.

The mirror error belongs to those who quote the commandment as a full theory of property. It is not. The same law that says thou shalt not steal says the land shall not be sold for ever, for the land is mine (Leviticus 25:23), and every Israelite held his field as a tenant of God on a fifty-year lease. Ownership in Scripture is real, protected, and derivative — a stewardship rather than an absolute dominion — which is why the same chapter that protects the field also commands its corners be left unharvested. And Ephesians 4:28 gives the commandment its evangelical form: the aim is not merely a man who no longer steals but a man who works in order to have something to give. That is more than restitution; it is the direction of a life reversed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ganab (to steal, take by stealth) and gannab (a thief); Greek klepto (to steal) and kleptes (a thief), distinct from lestes, a robber or bandit who uses force.

expand to see more

Hebrew ganab (H1589) — to steal, carry away by stealth; the verb of the eighth commandment.

Hebrew gannab (H1590) — a thief; the offender whose restitution is set out in Exodus 22:1-4.

Greek klepto (G2813) — to steal; the verb in Ephesians 4:28 and Matthew 6:19-20.

Greek kleptes (G2812) — a thief, one who takes by stealth; the word in John 10:10 and 1 Thessalonians 5:2.

Greek lestes (G3027) — a robber, bandit using violence; the word for Barabbas and for the two crucified with Christ.

Usage

"“Thou shalt not steal” — three words that presuppose real property and a real owner."

"“Let him labour… that he may have to give” — the thief's repentance ends in generosity, not merely in restraint."

"“Lest I be poor, and steal” — Agur prays against both riches and poverty, naming the temptation of each."
